1029-the-night-born:
Jack London gathers here a set of short tales from the edge of civilized life: prospectors, sailors, prize-fighters, and men who test themselves against cold, sea, and greed. The title points to those born, as London saw it, to roam by night and live by nerve rather than by rule. The stories range from the far north to the warm seas.

London's people face stark choices, and luck or pluck decides them in a few hard pages. His prose is blunt and fast, with a taste for strong men and stronger fates. The book shows his range beyond his famous dog tales, and it rewards readers who like short, sharp yarns.
10451-life-of-johnson-volume-5-tour-to-t:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, continues in this fifth volume with two journeys. One is the tour to the Hebrides in 1773. The other is Johnson's diary of a journey into North Wales in 1774. Boswell traveled with Johnson to Scotland, recording talk, anecdotes, and opinions of men and books along the way.

The volume adds Johnson's own poems on the tour, never before published. It also gives an authentic account of the escape of the grandson of James II in 1746. Hebridean islands, Welsh roads, and Johnson's conversation fill the pages. Readers get a classic travel biography, full of wit, landscape, and eighteenth-century life.
11327-english-literature-modern:
G. H. Mair's English Literature: Modern, in the Home University Library, surveys English writing from the Renaissance to the present age in ten short chapters. Elizabethan poetry and prose, the drama, the seventeenth century, the age of good sense, Dr. Johnson, the Romantic revival, the Victorian age, and the novel each get a chapter, with a bibliography and chronological table. First printed in 1911 and revised in 1914, the book was meant for general readers.

Mair opens by comparing literary ages to moments of sudden widening in a person's life, when new possibilities bring fresh endeavor. His judgments are brisk and confident, in the style of the series. Students still find the volume a useful short map of the field, even where later scholarship has revised its verdicts.
12190-the-adventures-of-captain-horn:
Frank R. Stockton published The Adventures of Captain Horn in 1910, an adventure novel that begins with a shipwreck and grows into a treasure hunt. Stockton, known for The Lady, or the Tiger, here mixes sea yarn with business comedy.

Captain Horn and his party, cast ashore in South America, face the Rackbirds, a gang of outlaws, and discover a hidden hoard. Chapters follow an introductory disaster, new faces in camp, a cliff scheme, and a pile of fuel that hides more than warmth. Horn must get his people home, guard the treasure, and deal honestly with partners and claimants. The novel is brisk and inventive, with Stockton usual calm narration of wild events.
12327-the-jewish-manual-practical-inform:
Edited by a lady and published in London in 1846, The Jewish Manual offers practical information in Jewish and modern cookery, with recipes and hints relating to the toilette. The editor preface notes that existing culinary works give no insight into the Hebrew kitchen.

Most cookbooks, she argues, are valueless to the Jewish housekeeper because of prohibited articles and combinations. The manual therefore gives kosher recipes, including Molina pie: minced cold veal or chicken with smoked beef or tongue, seasoned, simmered in gravy, and bound with egg yolks. It also covers table manners and dress. The book is an early English Jewish cookbook, practical, pioneering, and proud of its kitchen.
12777-the-young-engineers-in-nevada-or-s:
Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton try their luck as mining engineers in Nevada in this Hancock adventure. A boy named Alf, a trail camp, and Jim Ferrers, who becomes their partner, set the story going. Claims, new owners, and a rival named Dolph Gage test their nerve, while snow, wolves, and a signal of distress raise the stakes.

After losing the best claim in the district by being too slow, Tom resolves that they will stake their fortunes on the turn of a pick, working their own mines in earnest. Harry, at first downcast, falls in with the plan. The tale pairs mining craft with pluck and partnership.
12930-publications-of-the-scottish-histo:
Volume thirty-six of the Scottish History Society publications prints the journals of Sir John Lauder, Lord Fountainhall, from 1665 to 1676, edited by Donald Crawford. Journals in France, journeys in London, Oxford, and Scotland, and a chronicle of the Court of Session fill the volume. Observations on public affairs, accounts, a book catalogue, and a letter to his son complete it.

A Bedlam story shows the period flavour: a man who believed his head was glass was cured when attendants broke glass before him, proving the glass, not his head, had shattered. Fountainhall's notes give Restoration Scotland in a lawyer's sharp eye. The volume serves historians of seventeenth-century Scotland.
13077-wild-western-scenes-a-narrative-of:
J. B. Jones's narrative, first entered in 1856 and reissued in a revised stereotype edition in 1875, centers on Daniel Boone, the famed American pioneer. Jones frames Boone's exploits with tales of bear, deer, and buffalo hunts, wolf hunts, fishing, fights with Native peoples, and meetings with snakes. Sixteen engravings from original designs illustrate the text.

The story is told by a party traveling the western wilds, with Boone as guide and hero, and a talkative companion named Joe for comic relief. Campfire talk, strange sounds in the air, and sudden alarms on the trail fill the chapters. Jones wrote for readers hungry for frontier adventure, and his Boone is less a man of record than a legend made to carry the whole West.
13115-anahuac-or-mexico-and-the-mexicans:
Edward Burnett Tylor's 1861 travel book follows a route from Cuba through Yucatan and Vera Cruz into the heart of Mexico. Its chapter headings run from Cuban railways and pirates to Mexican politics, Aztec remains, aloe fields, and mud-brick houses. Tylor, later a founder of anthropology, writes as a curious traveler with an eye for custom.

He notes drinkers who take spirits hour by hour, potters at Soquital, and salt carriers on the road. A night ride brings a grand sight: grass fire sweeping a hillside, throwing light over smoke and cloud. Tylor mixes ancient and modern Mexico at every step, and the book remains a lively, if dated, portrait of a country on the edge of change.
14338-books-and-habits-from-the-lectures:
John Erskine chose and edited these lectures by Lafcadio Hearn, printed in 1922. Hearn taught English letters in Japan, and spoke to students who met Western books across a gap of tongue and custom. The lectures ask what makes a book hard to grasp, and how taste grows. They range over old Norse tales, French verse, and English prose. Hearn's voice is that of a teacher who loves books and trusts reading.

One lecture weighs Norse feud law, where a killing called for vengeance unless a blood price was paid. Hearn notes that kin seldom felt paid off by coin alone, so feuds could run for years. Another lecture lingers on a French poem about a cicada that sings till it dies on a stalk. Hearn glosses the word encolure, the line of neck and shoulder, for which English has no twin. The book opens two far-apart literatures through talk.
14844-the-taming-of-red-butte-western:
Francis Lynde's western, published by Scribner in 1916 from a 1910 copyright, sets out to tame Red Butte. Collars and cuffs, the red desert, a little brother of the cows and the Rio Gloria open a story of ranching, rail and rough men.

Outlaws, everyman's share, a killer, bridge timbers, Judson's joke and Flemister follow, with nemesis, pleasurers, bitter-sweet, blind signals and Eleanor intervening. A shadowgraph closes the arc. Dedicated to Charles Augustine Stickle, brother in deed though not by blood, the tale of his birthland mixes romance with the hard work of bringing order to a wild valley.
1620-the-lion-and-the-unicorn:
Richard Harding Davis's Lion and the Unicorn gathers stories dedicated to Lt-Col Arthur H. Lee, British military attache with the United States Army, in memory of hot days and hot corners. The title tale follows Prentiss, who holds a long lease on a house, through a story of empire, love, and war.

Other tales, from On the Fever Ship to The Last Ride Together, move between soldiers, sailors, and correspondents at the edge of empire. Davis writes with dash and sentiment. The collection is a period book of adventure, vivid in its day and still readable for its energy.
16343-beth-woodburn:
Maud Petitt's Beth Woodburn, published in Toronto in 1897 by William Briggs, was the author's first book, lovingly dedicated to her mother. It opens in Briarsfield, a pretty village in Norfolk County close to Lake Erie's shore, already grown almost to town size and dignity. Chapter one finds Beth at eighteen, and later chapters follow a dream of life, a question of whither Beth, Marie, love, varsity days, and an ending.

Death, love, and farewell mark the later chapters, as Beth grows from village girlhood toward adult choice. Petitt writes gentle Canadian domestic fiction in a clear, warm style. Readers who like coming-of-age tales from small-town Ontario will find a tender first novel.
18256-woodside-or-look-listen-and-learn:
Caroline Hadley, author of Children's Sayings and Stories of Old, wrote this children's nature book, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1902. Woodside, or Look, Listen, and Learn, opens with Longfellow's verses on Nature as an old nurse who takes a child upon her knee and shows a story book written by the Father. The book asks children to wander, look, and listen.

Chapters bring grandpapa's house, listening in the woods, and Tom's birds' eggs. Jack and the gardener, hiving the bees, and wasps and their ways follow. Charley Foster's pets, a talk with Aunt Lizzie, and after the rain close the set. Illustrations show the arrival at grandpapa's, the visit to the watch-dog, and the visit to the pony. Children get nature study as a visit: animals, bees, and woods met at a grandparent's house.
18458-star-born:
Andre Norton wrote this science fiction novel, published by Ace Books in New York. Star Born opens with a question from Tas Kordov's Record of the First Years. What of the children born on a new world? They will have no memories of Terra's green hills and blue seas. Will they be Terrans, or something else? The novel takes up that question as its theme.

The story opens with travelers sighting a cove from the sea, the first break in a cliff wall guarding a continent's interior. Dalgard Nordis, son of the colony, steers an outrigger with Sssuri in the bow, two voyagers of different race and species working without words, as if bound by a rapport beyond speech. Readers get a colony world seen through its second generation: exploration, alien friendship, and the making of a new people.
18565-a-little-swiss-sojourn:
W. D. Howells wrote this travel book, published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1893, with illustrations of Montreux, Villeneuve, the Castle of Chillon, and markets at Vevay. The book records eighty or ninety days passed in Switzerland, told in papers that follow the author's stay by the lake.

The first paper opens at the White Cross Inn, with tourists at Montreux and the road to Villeneuve. Howells writes of haymaking in the marshes, washing clothes in the lake, fountains, wine-presses, and bargains before a notary, giving a gentle, observant picture of Swiss town life in summer.
18855-the-return:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire published this science fiction story in Astounding Science Fiction in January 1954. It opens with a survey team in a helicopter over a yellow-brown river, eating a makeshift meal of smoked pork and rice. The crew, including Altamont and Loudons, is exploring country far from home.

The team soon finds a small, isolated group living on its own, whose religion strikes the visitors as strange, yet logical on its own terms. The story turns on that meeting: how a cut-off community keeps its beliefs, and how outsiders judge them. Readers get a short tale of exploration and cultural contact, told with Piper's usual care for practical detail.
19158-the-return:
H. Beam Piper and John J. McGuire wrote this science fiction tale, The Return, first printed in The Science-Fictional Sherlock Holmes in 1960. Altamont flies a helicopter over a yellow-brown river, eating a meal of smoked pork chops, rice, egg powder, and milk fried in bacon grease, cooked by Loudons from leftovers. The scene is a settled, walled town called the Toon.

Elders test young men with constant checks, while a leader of the Irregulars weighs whether to move the Toon, with its graves, walls, and houses that cannot travel. Theological disputes over sacred books add tension. Readers get a thoughtful post-collapse tale of tradition, leadership, and change.
19691-dead-man-s-plack-and-an-old-thorn:
A plack was an old Scots coin of small worth. Dead Man's Plack and An Old Thorn pairs two works of English local lore and nature writing. One passage follows a watcher haunting a spot day after day. He pursues small creatures, not to kill and cabinet them. He wants only to witness the comedy of their bright little lives.

That watcher sums up the book's spirit: patient, fond, and exact. English nature writing of this school prized the small and near. A thorn tree or a dead man's coin could anchor real feeling. The pieces reward slow reading. They record a countryside world that was already passing when they were written.
21058-the-strange-adventures-of-eric-bla:
Eric Blackburn, fourth officer of the steamship Saturn, tells his own story in Harry Collingwood's sea novel. When the Saturn is lost in mid-ocean, Blackburn is the sole survivor. A passing sailing ship picks him up, and he soon finds himself raised to skipper.

Blackburn joins a search for hidden treasure, and the search succeeds. On the way to port the ship is wrecked on an uncharted island. There he and the dead captain's son explore and meet a local king. They help that king fight off attacks by huge apes, then guard their treasure from two shady former crewmen.
21702-shifting-winds-a-tough-yarn:
Several linked tales run side by side in this sea story by R. M. Ballantyne, the Scottish writer of boys' adventure books. One thread follows the seaman Gaff and his son Billy, and another follows Mrs. Gaff at home. Captain Bingley, his son Gildart, the Stuart family, and a man named Haco Barepoles fill out the cast.

Most of the action stays ashore, in the small fishing village of Wreckumoft and the town of Athenbury. The book also shows the work of a charity that aided shipwrecked sailors and fishermen. Ballantyne weaves the separate lives together and apart, and the whole story carries a clear Christian message about duty, loss, and help given to strangers.
21789-a-discourse-of-life-and-death-by-m:
Two French works in the English of the Countess of Pembroke make up this volume, printed at London in 1592. The first is Philippe de Mornay's Discourse of Life and Death, a grave prose meditation. Mornay wonders why men hurry toward rest in every task, yet fear the end of life's own hard voyage. Life, he writes, is a sea open to all winds and a web forever woven and undone.

The second piece is Antonius, a tragedy by Robert Garnier, retelling the fall of Antony in classical form. Mary Sidney, the countess, was among the finest translators of her age. Her versions brought French thought and drama to English readers. The old spelling and stately pace reward slow reading.
22124-the-golden-shoemaker-or-cobbler-ho:
J. W. Keyworth tells a village tale in The Golden Shoemaker, or "Cobbler" Horn. Horn works in the little shop behind his kitchen. His house holds only two rooms below and three small chambers above. In the room over the workshop his wife lies dying, and her coughing sounds through the boarded floor.

Around this poor home Keyworth builds a story of faith, neighbours, and quiet endurance. The cobbler's nickname, and the gold of the title, point to worth that money cannot measure. Such tales were written for Sunday reading and cottage shelves. Keyworth's is a plain, tender example of Victorian religious fiction at its most domestic.
22358-erik-dorn:
Ben Hecht wrote Erik Dorn, a novel published in 1921. Hecht was a Chicago newspaperman turning to fiction. His hero is glimpsed first in darkness, watching people drift past a lawn.

Dorn lowers his eyes toward the street beyond the lawn. Figures seem to float under the dark trees. He cannot see them distinctly as they pass. At moments a face rewards his stare: a featureless glint of white. Shadows move within a motionless darkness around him. That moody opening suits a novel of ambition and city life. Hecht's sharp prose made Erik Dorn an early success in American letters.
22544-a-world-is-born:
Leigh Brackett wrote A World Is Born, a science fiction story of Mercury. Gray's fury opens the tale, hotter than boiling springs. Those springs run from the Sunside to water the valleys.

Gray hated John Moulton and his daughter Jill bitterly. They had conceived a plan of building a new world there. Their settlers would be destitute and desperate veterans of war. The Second Interplanetary War left those veterans needing a home. Building one on Mercury's twilight belt is their gamble and hope. Brackett was a master of planetary romance in the pulps. Her tale mixes harsh scenery, old soldiers, and stubborn colonization dreams.
23028-greylorn:
Keith Laumer opens Greylorn with a bleak report. Scouts went out forty-three years ago to all twenty-five colony worlds planted during the last century's Colonial Era. With the last scouts home, Earth faced the truth. No help, the report concludes, exists out there from any of them.

Cut off and weakening, humanity in Laumer's tale must look elsewhere for the help it needs. Greylorn names the grim errand that follows, a mission into dangers the report only hints at. Laumer wrote taut, ironic space adventure, and this novella shows his economy. Every paragraph earns its keep. Readers get a hard future, plainly told, with the stakes set in the first page.
23995-the-land-of-the-kangaroo-adventure:
Thomas W. Knox published The Land of the Kangaroo in Boston in 1896, subtitled The Adventures of Two Youths in the Great Island Continent. Knox, author of In Wild Africa and the fifteen-volume Boy Travelers series, died ten days after completing the book, leaving his planned travel series unfinished.

The publishers announced that remaining volumes would be issued by another hand. With five illustrations by H. Burgess, including a ship becalmed in the doldrums, the book follows two youths through Australia, then rapidly rising in prominence among the colonies. For boy readers of the 1890s, it was a first-hand-feeling tour of a continent of strange beasts and wide distances.
24248-the-girl-scouts-good-turn:
Edith Lavell wrote this girls' school story, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York in 1922. It belongs to her Girl Scouts series, beside The Girl Scouts at Miss Allen's School, The Girl Scouts at Camp, The Girl Scouts' Canoe Trip, and The Girl Scouts' Rivals. The tale is set at Miss Allen's Boarding School, where the girls return for the fall term.

On the first Saturday of term, the sophomores prepare their reception for the freshmen, with Marjorie Wilkinson as chairman. The bare gymnasium vanishes under cedar branches, artificial snow, snowbanks, pine needles, and frosty tinsel, with a dancing space kept clear in the middle. Readers get a cheerful school story of planning, friendship, and a good turn done well.
24567-blind-man-s-lantern:
Allen Kim Lang wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in Analog in December 1962 and illustrated by Schelling. Its premise is that successful colonies among the stars need interstellar ships, but they also need a rare sort of man, not the sort one might expect.

The story opens with an old village tale: a young man walking home in the dark meets a blind man carrying a lamp. The youngster shouts across the road, asking why a blind man needs light. Lang turns that parable into a story of space colonisation. Readers get a clever, humane tale about the unseen work that keeps a colony alive.
26342-chronicles-of-strathearn:
Chronicles of Strathearn, published at Crieff by David Philips in 1896 with pictures by W. B. MacDougall, gathers local history from many ministerial pens. Contents list Celtic saints and ancient churches, the Pictish capital, the historic presbytery of Auchterarder, memories of Gask, and the head of Strathearn. Later pieces cover the banks of the Devon, the well of Saint Fillan, the plain of the bards, and the abbey of Inchaffray.

A southern outpost on the Highland edge, the castle and sheriffdom of Auchterarder, and the gate of the Highlands close the set. The opening piece recalls sunset on the Knock of Crieff, with afterglow lying like purple mist from Ben Ledi to Comrie. The book gives a Scottish valley its past in short, vivid chapters.
26417-a-sheaf-of-corn:
Mary E. Mann's 1908 collection gathers short stories of English village life around the fictional Dulditch. The opening tale finds Dinah Brome in the village shop, watching the weighing of her weekly groceries with keen eyes. Strong and wholesome in looks, sober in dress, she pays well and constantly, yet the narrator insists she lacks any backbone of character.

Other stories follow a clerk, a tea-shop, a chalk mark on a gate, Freddy's ship, a nerve cure, a private ward, and Dora of the ringlets. Pink carnations, a little white dog, a broken boot, and the cares of a curate round out the sheaf. Mann's sketches are sharp, unsentimental, and fond of exposing the gap between respectable looks and inner worth.
26673-at-the-sign-of-the-jack-o-lantern:
Myrtle Reed published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap at New York, copyrighted in 1902, issued under arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. Reed was already known for Lavender and Old Lace, The Master's Violin, and A Spinner in the Sun. Its first chapter is called The End of the Honeymoon, and its last The Love of Another Elaine.

Dorothy and Harlan arrive by stage in a blinding storm at a queer house with eccentric outlines. The driver calls out good luck and the Jack-o'-Lantern as he leaves them. Matches sputter and fail in the empty, echoing rooms until a candle is found. Later chapters bring a first caller, finances, Mrs. Smithers, the coming of Elaine, an uninvited guest, Mrs. Dodd's husbands and fates, treasure-trove, and Uncle Ebeneezer's diary.
2766-the-red-acorn:
John McElroy wrote this Civil War novel of a young Union volunteer learning war the hard way. The red acorn of the title marks a corps badge, and the hero's journey runs from enlistment and fear through battle, shame, and hard won courage.

McElroy, himself a veteran, writes with blunt honesty about camp life, combat, and the men who broke or held. The novel mixes adventure with moral weight, and it avoids easy glory. It remains a respected story of the war from a private's view, told by one who knew it.
3075-the-return:
Walter de la Mare wrote The Return as a supernatural novel opening with a warning from Sir Thomas Browne against seeking roses in Attalus's garden or wholesome flowers in a venomous plantation. The book runs to twenty-three chapters, beginning in a churchyard. Arthur Lawford, a respectable man, falls asleep on a grave and wakes changed, possessed by the spirit of a dead man.

A stranger offers Lawford more of the dead man's history than the sexton knows, inviting him to a house at the foot of the hill, not half a mile distant. Lawford takes out his watch and considers the offer. The novel's horror lies in identity itself, as one man's life invades another's. It remains de la Mare's most haunting long fiction.
318-john-barleycorn:
Jack London voted on a warm California election day after several drinks, then rode home for another. John Barleycorn, published in 1913, opens in the Valley of the Moon, where London's wife Charmian asks how he voted on suffrage. His answer surprises her.

London traces his lifelong wrestle with drink, from youthful bravado to tolerant acceptance and finally to warning. Barleycorn, his name for alcohol, appears as a cunning companion and enemy. The memoir mixes confession, humor, and temperance argument. It remains a frank classic on addiction. London's memoir helped the temperance cause he came to support.
3417-the-fortunes-of-oliver-horn:
Francis Hopkinson Smith sets this novel in Baltimore, opening on Kennedy Square in the late eighteen fifties. The square holds birds, trees, flowers, and old stone benches, with great magnolias scenting the air and roses climbing the railings. At its center stands the old house of Richard Horn, a noted inventor whom the book calls the man least understood.

His son Oliver grows up in that house and must make his own way as an artist and a man. Smith follows Oliver through studios, friendships, and love, against a city that is itself changing. The novel mixes a coming of age story with a portrait of old Baltimore, and it suits readers who enjoy rich settings and a hero shaped by family pride.
369-the-outlaw-of-torn:
Edgar Rice Burroughs frames this medieval tale as a lost chronicle dug from a monastery in Europe. The story claims to tell of Richard, a lost prince of England, hidden and wronged in the reign of Henry III. A quarrel between king and Simon de Montfort sets the plot in motion in June 1243.

The prince grows into the visored horseman of Torn, a feared outlaw who rights wrongs by sword. Burroughs keeps the action brisk, with castle plots, chases, and duels. The book works as a bold romance of revenge and hidden birth, told in the guise of history found by chance.
616-prayers-written-at-vailima-and-a-low:
Robert Louis Stevenson writes family prayers for his Samoan household in this small volume, with an introduction by his wife. Evening prayer and hymns closed each Samoan day, and Stevenson, three miles above Apia at Vailima, joined the rite with thanks for home, food, friends, and work. Prayers for success, grace, rain, friends, and renewal fill the pages.

A Lowden Sabbath Morn, a Scots poem, follows the prayers. Stevenson's words are plain, warm, and direct, asking for courage, gaiety, and a quiet mind. The book charms as a glimpse of the writer at home, where faith was a daily habit, not a Sunday show.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-bene:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Benedictbeurn describes a Bavarian abbey in the Alps, about thirty miles south of Munich, formerly in the diocese of Augsburg. Tradition and tenth-century manuscripts ascribe its foundation in 740 to three noble brothers, Lanfrid, Wulfram and Eliland, acting under St. Boniface, then preaching in Bavaria.

The Huns destroyed the house in 955 or 973, and Wolfold restored it in 969 as a college of canons. Through Emperor Henry the Third, Abbot Ellinger and eleven monks from Tegernsee revived Benedictine rule there in 1031. The entry follows the abbey's later fortunes, its abbots and its standing among Bavarian monasteries, and settles its much-varied spelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durandus-of-t:
Durandus of Troarn was a French Benedictine and church writer born about 1012 near Evreux. He died at Troarn near Caen in 1089. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he was given from childhood to the communities of Mont-Sainte-Catherine and Saint-Vandrille. William, Duke of Normandy, made him abbot of the new Saint-Martin of Troarn, esteeming him alongside Lanfranc, Anselm, and Gerbert.

Ordericus Vitalis calls him a most skilled teacher of church song and doctrine, though of his music nothing survives but the praise. His Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord answers Berengarius, and its ninth part holds precious history of the heretic. The entry adds his epitaphs for Abbot Ainard and Countess Mabile, preserved by Migne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-born:
The first-born son held pride of place in ancient Israel, with a double share and his father's blessing. Before the Law, the birthright also carried a right to the priesthood of the household. First-born sons and firstling animals were held to be God's in a special way. Among nomad tribes this belief likely gave rise to sacrificing the first-cast animals.

Under the Law, every first-born son was redeemed one month after birth for five sicles. The payment went to the clergy and recalled the slaying of Egypt's first-born at the Exodus. The firstling of clean animals was sacrificed at a year old; unclean animals were redeemed with money. Polygamy forced precise rules on which child counted as first-born and which child was redeemed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiherr-max-:
Max von Gagern, a Nassau statesman born in 1810, spent the revolutionary year of 1848 trying to unite Germany under Prussia without Austria. Son of a Nassau minister, he studied law at Heidelberg, Utrecht, and Göttingen. He served the Dutch king, fought against Belgium in 1830, and later taught history at Bonn. He entered the Catholic Church in August 1843.

His conversion grew from reading Thomas à Kempis, Möhler, and the New Testament, and it cost him nothing with his duke. In 1848 he mediated between governments and people, chaired a committee of seventeen revising the constitution, and served as under-secretary for foreign affairs. When Prussia refused the imperial crown, he withdrew from the Frankfurt parliament with his party.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gertrude-of-h:
Gertrude of Hackeborn, Cistercian Abbess of Helfta, made her convent Germany's home of asceticism and mysticism. Born near Halberstadt in 1232 to the noble Hackeborns and sister to Saint Mechtild, she entered Rodersdorf young and was elected abbess in 1251 aged nineteen. In 1253 she founded Hedersleben with her brothers Albert and Louis.

Wanting water, Gertrude obtained her brothers' castle of Helfta and moved her community there in 1258. Under her rule Helfta became Germany's most famous abode of asceticism and mysticism, its nuns trained in liberal arts and above all in Scripture. A model abbess for piety and prudent direction, she bore apoplexy in her last eighteen months with heroic patience until her death near the end of 1292. She must not be confused with Saint Gertrude the Great, an ordinary nun of the same house born over twenty years later. For this abbess wrote nothing, claimed no revelations, and was never canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goulburn:
Goulburn is one of the six suffragan sees of the ecclesiastical province of Sydney in New South Wales, Australia. Its episcopal city, population 10,612 in 1901, straddles the Sydney-Melbourne railroad at 2071 feet above the sea. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese watered by the Murrumbidgee, Murray, and Lachlan.

Formed as a separate diocese in 1864 from Sydney, it first went to Bonaventure Geoghegan, who died in Ireland that year without taking possession. His successor William Lanigan, consecrated at Goulburn in 1867, was the first Australian bishop consecrated in his own cathedral and an ardent promoter of Catholic education. By November 1908 the diocese counted fifty-nine priests, twenty-four parochial districts, and hundreds of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-anton-z:
Jacob Anton Zallinger zum Thurn was a philosopher and canonist from Bozen. He was born there on 26 July 1735. He died there on 11 January 1813. He studied at Innsbruck and Munich. He joined the Jesuits on 9 October 1753. He was ordained priest on 1 June 1765. He then taught philosophy at Munich, Dillingen, and Innsbruck.

After the Jesuits were suppressed in 1773, Prince-bishop Clemens Wenceslaus hired him. He taught canon law at Augsburg for thirty years, from 1777 to 1807. He spent four months as theologian at the Ratisbon nunciature. He also spent sixteen months in Rome as papal councillor on German affairs. As a canonist he defended papal rights against Febronian trends. As a philosopher he favored Newton's empiricism over Scholastic method.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-pfef:
Johannes Pfefferkorn was a converted Jew whose campaign against Jewish books set off the great Reuchlin controversy. Born probably at Nuremberg in 1469, he was baptized at Cologne in 1505 with his wife and children, then pressed for the conversion of the Jews. His Judenspiegel of 1507 urged Jews to give up usury, work for a living, attend Christian sermons, and abandon the Talmud, while condemning persecution as a bar to conversion.

Convinced that Jewish books were the root of Jewish obstinacy, he won an imperial order in 1509 to seize them and began confiscations at Frankfurt, Worms, Mainz, and other towns. A second mandate put the affair under the Archbishop of Mainz, who sought opinions from universities and from Johann Reuchlin. Reuchlin defended all but openly offensive books, and the quarrel with Pfefferkorn and the Cologne Dominicans became a landmark dispute over learning, tolerance, and the treatment of Jews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-annega:
Joseph Annegarn was a German Catholic theologian and popular writer who lived from 1794 to 1843. Born at Ostbevern in Westphalia, he became professor of church history at the Lyceum Hosianum in Braunsberg, East Prussia, where he died. His service to German Catholic letters came chiefly through a history written for young readers and the general public.

His Universal History, published in eight volumes between 1827 and 1829, told world history from a frankly Catholic view in a bright, pleasing style. Character sketches of great figures and chronological tables were its best features, and later editors kept it current, so it stayed a standard book in German Catholic homes. He also wrote a handbook of patrology, the study of the Church Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-gasser:
Joseph Gasser von Valhorn was an Austrian sculptor who lived from 1816 to 1900. Born at Prägraten in Tyrol, he learned woodcarving from his father, studied at the Vienna Academy, and spent years in Rome on a government stipend. Settled in Vienna from 1852, he carved five heroic figures for Speyer Cathedral's portal and reliefs for its Kaiserhalle.

His other works include statues for the Arsenal museum, the Seven Liberal Arts for the Opera House staircase, and twenty-four figures for St. Stephen's Cathedral. His finest group serves Vienna's Votive Church: the Coronation of Mary, the Trinity, and Christ the Redeemer. He taught at the Academy from 1865 to 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lantern:
In modern architecture a lantern is a small structure crowning a dome to let in light, aid ventilation, and ornament the building. The name also covers any such projection, even one with no openings that serves decoration alone.

Examples span Europe and beyond: the Karlskirche in Vienna, St. Peter's in Rome, St. Paul's in London, St. Isaac's in St. Petersburg, Santa Maria della Salute in Venice, Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence, the Frauenkirche in Dresden, Val de Grace in Paris, St. Stephen's Walbrook in London, La Superga in Turin, and Palermo cathedral, with others at Montepulciano, Loyola, Genoa, and Guadalupe in Mexico.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lectern:
A lectern, from Latin legere, to read, is a bookstand, a solid permanent structure holding the large heavy Sacred Books for ministers at liturgical functions. Early churches used one only, later two: one at the choir's north wall, another opposite.

From the first, the priest preached and the bishop spoke, unless from his cathedra. Synod decrees were proclaimed there, censures and excommunications pronounced, diptychs read, and the deacon chanted the Gospel and his own liturgical parts. The second, longer but lower, split into two levels. The higher, facing the altar, served the subdeacon's Epistle. The lower, facing the nave, served other lessons. Some were marble, others wood adorned with silver, gold, enamel, gems, bronze, and ivory, and eagle-shaped lecterns spread widely in thirteenth- and fourteenth-century England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liesborn:
Liesborn was a noted former Benedictine Abbey in Westphalia, Germany, begun in 815 and suppressed in 1803. More likely two laymen, Bozo and Bardo, built it in 815. As time passed the nuns grew worldly, so in 1131 Bishop Egbert of Munster expelled them and put Benedictine monks in their place.

From the thirteenth century ascetic life declined as its wealth grew. The Bursfeld Union worked here in 1465 for discipline's restoration. To it Liesborn owed its flourishing state under abbots Heinrich of Cleves (1464-1490) and Johann Smalebecker, abbot 1490-1522, who restored the buildings and improved its economics. Abbot Heinrich's fine altar-paintings became famous, but under French rule in 1807 they sold for a mere song. Bernard Witte, a monk from 1490 to about 1534, wrote a history of Westphalia and an abbey chronicle. Under Johann Rodde (1582-1601) decay grew again, and things were worse during the seventeenth century's wars, until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malvern:
Malvern was a district in Worcestershire under a lofty range between the Severn and the Wye, the Malvern Hills. On the range's eastern side stood two Benedictine houses, the priories of Great and Little Malvern. This entry follows both houses through their tangled fortunes.

Great Malvern grew up soon after St Werstan's death; the Deerhurst monk was slain by Danes in the woods and honoured as a saint. A hermitage predated the Conquest, and Aldwyn, a Worcester monk, with a companion named Guy, first settled the site. At St Wulstan's counsel Aldwyn dropped a planned Jerusalem pilgrimage and began a monastery, gathering thirty monks. Later a bishop's harsh claims sparked long litigation, with monks at last under royal protection, until a truce at Acton Burnell freed them from his jurisdiction. Little Malvern, founded from Worcester about 1171, keeps only its choir and tower today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osbern:
Osbern of Canterbury was a monk, prior of Christ Church, and writer of saints' lives who died probably between 1088 and 1093. Brought up by Godric, dean from 1058 to 1080, he was ordained by Archbishop Lanfranc and grew skilled in music. Two music treatises are linked to his name, though his fame rests on hagiography, the writing of saints' lives.

William of Malmesbury praised the elegance of his style. Osbern turned Anglo-Saxon lives into Latin and wrote fresh ones of his own. His works include lives of Alphege and Dunstan, with a book of Dunstan's miracles, and a life of Archbishop Odo that has perished. A life of Dunstan printed under his name in Mabillon probably belongs to Eadmer instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paderborn:
Paderborn is a suffragan diocese of Cologne, taking in Minden and Arnsberg in Westphalia, Prussian Saxony, five Rhine districts, Lippe, Waldeck, Gotha, both Schwarzburgs, and the Vicariate Apostolic of Anhalt. It holds 53 deaneries, 547 parishes, 1,403 secular priests, 93 regular priests, 1,508,000 Catholics, and 5,250,000 non-Catholics. The diocese is large and mixed, with Catholics a minority among its people.

The cathedral chapter elects the bishop, and diocesan schools include a priests' seminary, an institute of philosophy and theology, the Leoninum college, and boys' seminaries at Paderborn and Heiligenstadt. Catholic charities run 120 child-protection homes, 50 orphan asylums, and many trade schools. Later pages trace the bishops from early foundations through the Thirty Years War to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-kentige:
Kentigern, also called Mungo, meaning dear one, was bishop and founder of the see of Glasgow. He was born about 518 and died at Glasgow on 13 January 603. His mother Thenaw was daughter of the British prince Lothus, and his father's name is unknown.

Brought up by Serf at Culross in Fife, according to Jocelyn's life, he began mission work at twenty-five at Cathures on the Clyde, the site of modern Glasgow. King Roderick of Strathclyde welcomed him and had him consecrated bishop about 540. He lived austerely in a cell where the Clyde meets the Molendinar, and a community called Clasgu, the dear family, grew around him into the town of Glasgow. Driven out about 553, he founded a monastery at Llanelwy, now Saint Asaph's, and returned after the battle of Arthuret in 573.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schaftlarn:
Schäftlarn, once Premonstratensian and now Benedictine, is an abbey on the Isar not far from Munich in Upper Bavaria. Priest Waltrich founded it in 762 for St Dionysius and served as first abbot, later becoming bishop of Passau from 774 to 804. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a house destroyed, refounded, secularised, and reborn.

Hungarians wrecked the monastery in 955 during their raids into Germany. In the eleventh century secular canons held it, until Bishop Otto of Freising refounded it in 1140 as a Premonstratensian house under a provost. Fire destroyed it in 1527, the provostry became an abbey in 1598, and secularisation ended it in 1803. After years as a girls' school, King Louis I bought it in 1865 and restored Benedictine life in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schonborn:
Schönborn names a German noble family rich in church prelates, above all Johann Philipp von Schönborn, who ruled Mainz as archbishop and held the bishoprics of Würzburg and Worms. Born at Eschbach in the Westerwald on 6 August 1605, he died at Würzburg on 12 February 1673. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a prince-bishop of the Thirty Years' War aftermath.

At sixteen he became an expectant cleric at Würzburg cathedral, then at Mainz in 1625. He became canon at Würzburg in 1629 and Worms in 1630, and provost of Kronberg and St Burkard in 1635. Bishop of Würzburg in 1642, deacon that year and priest in 1645, he became archbishop of Mainz in 1647 and bishop of Worms in 1663. His foreign policy sought peace, often without success or applause, but his home rule was excellent, earning him the titles Wise, German Solomon, and Cato of Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solomon-islan:
The Northern Solomon Islands prefecture covered Ysabel, Choiseul, Bougainville, and the smaller islets under German protection in the western Pacific. This entry records its early mission years. Placed under the vicar apostolic of Samoa in 1897, it became a prefecture of its own in 1898. Mgr Joseph Forestier led it from Kieta on Bougainville.

By 1911 the mission counted three churches and three stations. It had Marist fathers and lay brothers, sisters of the Third Order of Mary, and Samoan catechists. Five schools taught 140 pupils, and two orphanages served a few hundred Catholics. Fever, the entry notes frankly, had already carried off most of the fathers who arrived in 1898. That loss is a grim reminder of the human cost of the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-ea:
Eastern Sze-ch'wan became a Vicariate Apostolic in 1856, after separation from the northwest, and was first called South-eastern Sze-ch'wan. Nine European and ten native priests served it under its first vicar, Desflèches, bishop of Sinita, who led it from 1844 to 1887. Early years brought heavy persecution, until the Franco-Chinese War of 1860 won full freedom to preach.

In 1860 the mission split into Eastern and Southern vicariates, and Chinese officials granted land at Ch'ung-k'ing as compensation for losses. Fresh violence followed: priests were jailed and murdered, settlements were pillaged in 1876, and mission buildings at Ch'ung-k'ing were wrecked in 1886. By 1910 the Paris Foreign Missions vicariate counted 40,587 Catholics, 341 schools, and 175 churches under Bishop Chouvellon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-no:
North-western Sze-ch'wan covers Ch'wan-si and Ch'-wan-pe, with Kiong-chu, Ya-y-hien, Mu-pin, and part of Tsechu prefecture, among 25,000,000 people, of whom 23,000,000 are Chinese and 1,500,000 Man-tse. Rome entrusted the whole Sze-ch'wan mission to Bishop Pallu in 1658, but neither he nor his successor Lyonne could enter the province. Only in 1707 did Paris missionaries and Vincentians reach it.

La Balluère, elected vicar in 1713, died before consecration, Mullener was consecrated in 1717, and four later electees never reached consecration at all. Real organized life dates only from Bishop Pottier, consecrated in 1769, when the mission counted about 4,000 Christians. Persecution, banishment, and a synod that completed its organization followed, and by 1910 it counted 45,000 Catholics with 340 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sze-ch-wan-so:
Southern Sze-ch'wan became a Vicariate Apostolic on 24 January 1860, separated from the east by decree of Pius IX. Its first vicar, Pichon, bishop of Heliopolis, began with 12,000 Catholics, himself the only European missionary, plus three native priests and four chapels. He founded a seminary at Ho-ti-keou in 1862 and died in France in 1871, succeeded by Lepley.

Violence scarred the mission: Protestant buildings at Chen-tu fell in May 1895, Catholic settlements followed the next day, and about half the mission's settlements were destroyed. A new persecution broke out in 1898, the Boxers spared it somewhat in 1900, and some thirty Christians were murdered between 1895 and 1904. By 1910, under Bishop Chatagnon at Sui-fu, it counted 36,618 Catholics and 280 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-master-of:
An unnamed Westphalian painter, known only by his masterpiece, is the subject of this art entry. In 1465 he painted a noted altar-piece for the Benedictine monastery of Liesborn, founded by Charlemagne. The monastery's historian, silent on his name, judged that Greeks would have ranked him first among artists. Westphalia already rivalled Cologne in the fourteenth century.

Against Stephen Lochner of Cologne, the Liesborn master holds his own, sharing with him and the Van Eycks a backward-looking grace rather than a forward thrust. Suppression in 1807 scattered the altar-piece, sold and split into fragments now in London's National Gallery, Münster Museum, and private hands. A copy at Luenen hints at its lost glory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-of-win:
Walter of Winterburn was an English Dominican cardinal, orator, poet, philosopher, and theologian of the thirteenth century, dying at Genoa on 26 August 1305. Entering the Dominicans young, he became renowned for learning, prudence.

In 1305, after helping elect Clement V, he set out from Perugia with other cardinals to join the pope in France. Fell mortally ill at Genoa, attended by Nicholas de Prato, dean of the Sacred College. First buried in his order's Genoa church, his remains were later transferred to London as he had ordered, to the convent where he had served. His friend Nicholas Trivet testifies to his many superior qualities, rare modesty, kindly disposition, and mature learning, and to prayer hours never shortened despite cloister and court duties. His chief works include a commentary on the Sentences and theological questions much used in his day.
doe-osti-2585504-a-short-survey-of-curre: Reactive burn models got their mid-2025 survey, and this DOE report covers current capabilities. The pages detail the short survey. The explosives modelers get their status. The year was mid-2025. The capabilities were reactive burn. The status was modeler. The survey was short.
doe-osti-2588783-flexible-fuel-electric-: Glass furnaces got their flexible-fuel hybrid demo, and this DOE report covers the electric hybrid. The pages detail the demonstration. The glassmakers get their option. The furnace was flexible fuel. The demonstration was furnace. The makers got options. The demo was glass.
doe-osti-3000976-tracking-carbon-dioxide: Southern Ocean CO2 got tracked, and this DOE final covers the technical findings. The pages detail the carbon measurements. The ocean folks get their closeout. The ocean was Southern. The closeout was ocean. The measurements were carbon. The closeout was ocean.
doe-osti-3004689-probabilistic-hazard-as: Tornado hazards got probabilistically assessed, and this DOE text covers Savannah River. The pages detail the wind findings. The safety folks get their numbers. The hazards were tornado and wind. The numbers were safety. The site was Savannah River. The wind was straight-line.
doe-osti-3009034-the-hydropower-game-an-: The Hydropower Game got interactive, and this DOE tool teaches the future workforce. The pages detail the learning design. The educators get their game. The workforce was future hydropower. The game was educator. The tool was interactive. The design was learning.
doe-osti-3487001-cloud-based-demonstrati: ESAMS got cloud-demonstrated, and this DOE text covers eastern interconnection awareness. The pages detail the cloud findings. The grid folks get their data. The system was situational. The data were grid. The interconnection were eastern. The ESAMS were demonstration.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Cub:
United States trade sanctions on Cuba reached their sixtieth year, and the Archive marked the date by posting its own documents on the embargo's start. One early statement of intent is quoted in full. The goal was to bring about hunger, desperation, and the overthrow of the Castro government.

That plain wording is why the posting matters. Sanctions are often defended in mild language about pressure and change. The founding documents say something harsher, aimed at daily life on the island. Readers can judge six decades of policy against the purpose its authors wrote down at the beginning.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Early Atomic Energy Commission studies warned that gas centrifuges could spread nuclear weapons with ease. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 385, published in June 2012. The studies said it would not be too difficult to build a secret plant producing highly enriched uranium.

Unless the United States and its allies imposed classification and export controls, officials feared, unfriendly countries such as China could acquire centrifuges. History proved the warning right: centrifuge technology later powered several secret programs. Reading the early studies shows the risk was understood in detail decades before it dominated headlines, and that controls were the chosen answer from the start.
john-barleycorn:
John Barleycorn is Jack London's book about his own life with alcohol, published in 1913. John Barleycorn is the old name for drink itself, treated here as a person. The book opens on an election day in California's Valley of the Moon. London rides down from his ranch to vote, taking several drinks before and after his ballot.

At supper, his wife Charmian asks why he voted for women's suffrage. He answers at length: women, he says, will vote for prohibition and drive nails into John Barleycorn's coffin. Yet he calls drink both the king of liars and the frankest truth-teller. That split feeling, friend and foe at once, drives this honest memoir of a drinking life.
life-of-johnson-volume-5-tour-to-the-heb:
Volume Five holds Boswell's Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides. Johnson accompanied him through Scotland in 1773. The volume adds Johnson's diary of a journey into North Wales in 1774. Hill's six-volume edition frames both travel records together.

Boswell's journal prints poems by Johnson about the tour. Conversations, literary anecdotes, and opinions of men and books follow. An authentic account covers the Jacobite grandson's distresses and escape in 1746. This third edition of the journal was revised and corrected. Poetical pieces by Johnson about the tour appear here first. The Jacobite escape account adds highland history to the travels.
prayers-written-at-vailima-and-a-lowden-:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Prayers Written at Vailima appear here with an introduction by his widow, in the Chatto and Windus edition of 1916, bound with his poem A Lowden Sabbath Morn. Stevenson wrote the prayers in Samoa for the evening service of his household at Vailima. His widow explains that every Samoan household closes the day with prayer and hymns, and that omitting the duty would shame the house chief. Her introduction compares the average Samoan to a larger child at his mother's knee, going to bed with a sense of heavenly protection.

The prayers themselves are short, plain, and tender, written to be spoken aloud by a family and its servants under a Samoan roof. A Lowden Sabbath Morn, a Scots poem of a quiet Sunday in the Lowlands, carries the homesick counterweight. Together they show the private Stevenson: the unbeliever's son who became, in exile, a patriarch of prayer.
publications-of-the-scottish-history-soc:
Donald Crawford edited the journals of Sir John Lauder, Lord Fountainhall, for the Scottish History Society in a volume dated May 1900. Lauder kept notes on public affairs and private matters between 1665 and 1676, a span of travel and early legal life.

The contents list a journal in France from 1665 to 1667, journeys in London, Oxford, and Scotland, a chronicle of the Court of Session, and remarks on public affairs. An appendix adds his accounts and a catalogue of his books. Readers get a young Scots lawyer's sharp record of courts, roads, and books.
star-born:
Andre Norton opens Star Born with a quote from Tas Kordov's Record of the First Years. What of our children, Kordov asks, the second and third waves born on this new world? They will hold no memories of Terra's green hills and blue seas. Will they be Terrans, or something else? Ace Books printed the novel at New York, and a note says deep searching found no proof that its copyright was renewed.

Chapter 1, Shooting Star, brings two travelers to a cove sighted from the sea. Dalgard steers an outrigger into the narrow break in the cliff wall, his paddle in time with Sssuri's in the bow. The two are neither of the same race nor of the same species, yet they work as one without words. Dalgard Nordis is a son of the Colony, whose Terran outlaw forebears fled foes across the galaxy to win a foothold on Astra.
the-adventures-of-captain-horn: Frank R. Stockton wrote The Adventures of Captain Horn. This copy is a 1910 printing. Its chapter list opens with An Introductory Disaster. The Rackbirds and Three Wild Beasts follow. The Captain Explores and A New Hemisphere come next. A Tradition and a Waistcoat stands midway. Mine, The Cliff-Maka Scheme, and Mrs. Cliff is Amazed close the parts shown.
the-fortunes-of-oliver-horn:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote The Fortunes of Oliver Horn as a novel of old Baltimore, giving the book to the memory of Richard Horn, a famed inventor little understood. Kennedy Square frames the tale.

Smith paints the square of the late fifties as a place of birds, trees, magnolias, and climbing roses. Boys and girls play by day while old gentlemen read in the shade. Watermelon men and oyster sellers work the pave outside the fence. In that soft, fading world the Horn family rises and falls, and young Oliver must make his way as art and trade change the town around him.
the-great-return: Arthur Machen wrote The Great Return. The Faith Press published it in London in 1915. Machen is named as author of The Bowmen. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a list of his other books, and a contents list. The contents name two pieces: The Rumour of the Marvellous and Odours of Paradise. No page of the tale itself is present. Its story cannot be told from what is here.
the-jewish-manual-practical-information-:
An anonymous lady edited this manual in London in 1846. It joins Jewish cookery with modern dishes. Hints on the toilette come with it. Her preface states the gap plainly. Many works on cookery existed already. None gave insight into the Hebrew kitchen. General cookbooks failed the Jewish housekeeper. Banned foods and mixes filled nearly every dish. Such books were useless to her.

The receipts came down by memory and manuscript. One generation of Jewish women passed them to the next. Plain English dishes join them here. French dishes from refined modern tables follow. Most were tested in the editor's own kitchen. Care went to accuracy and cheapness. Hard and costly methods were left out on purpose. Those belong to the confectioner, she says. Her aim was to guide the young Jewish housekeeper.
the-laughing-cavalier-the-story-of-the-a: Baroness Orczy published her tale of a Scarlet Pimpernel ancestor with Doran in New York in 1914. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The list names an apology and a prologue. Early chapters cover New Year Eve, a fracas by a postern gate, and watch night. The Dutch adventure itself, with its laughing cavalier and the brother and sister of later chapters, does not appear in this record.
the-lion-and-the-unicorn:
Richard Harding Davis gathers five war and adventure stories under his title piece. A florist named Prentiss keeps a shop in Jermyn Street, London, with a lion and a unicorn fixed over the front. Lodgings for single gentlemen fill the upper floors, as was usual on that street.

Captain Carrington moves in when the carved beasts arrive, and they watch his room by day and night. Maps and flag pins cover his table by day, while gold, silver, and soda bottles crowd it after dark. Other tales cover a fever ship, a vagrant, and a last ride together.
the-night-born:
Jack London's collection The Night-Born lists ten stories in its contents. The Madness of John Harned, When the World Was Young, The Benefit of the Doubt, Winged Blackmail, and Bunches of Knuckles follow the title story. War, Under the Deck Awnings, To Kill a Man, and The Mexican complete the set.

The title story opens in the old Alta-Inyo Club on a warm San Francisco night. Talk runs from the Graft Prosecution through the sordidness of man-hate until someone names O'Brien, the promising young pugilist who died in the prize-ring the night before. The air freshens at once: O'Brien neither drank, smoked, nor swore, and carried his prayer-book to the ringside. Old Trefethan, bald and dewlapped, takes up a Thoreau quotation and begins a tale from 1898.
the-outlaw-of-torn:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Outlaw of Torn, a tale of thirteenth-century England. The contents list nineteen chapters. In Chapter One the narrator explains that the story lay dormant for seven hundred years, first suppressed by a Plantagenet king, then forgotten. He found it among mildewed manuscripts in an ancient European monastery, through his wife's cousin, a Father Superior.

The manuscript records a remarkable revenge and the life of its innocent victim, Richard, the lost prince of England. Burroughs says he left out most of the history to follow the man at the center, a visored horseman. The events, he claims, shook England from north to south.
the-red-acorn: John McElroy is named as author on the electronic edition header. The header also gives the title. It gives an August 2001 release date. A later update followed in February 2018. Only that header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the story itself appears here. Nothing about the plot can be told from these pages alone.
the-return:
Walter de la Mare opens in an old churchyard on a mild golden September afternoon, where Arthur Lawford wanders among stones in keen, mellow silence. Robins sing across the graves, and Lawford seems to himself the only living creature present.

A motto from Sir Thomas Browne warns against seeking wholesome flowers in a venomous plantation or risking contagion by nearness to corruption. Twenty-three untitled chapters are listed before the prose begins. Readers should not confuse this quiet, uncanny novel with the science fiction story of the same short title elsewhere in the set.
the-taming-of-red-butte-western: Francis Lynde wrote The Taming of Red Butte Western, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1910 and dedicated to Charles Augustine Stickle, his brother in deed if not by blood. Front matter and a contents list are all that this record holds. Sixteen chapters run from Collars-and-Cuffs and The Red Desert through outlaws, a killer, bridge-timbers, and blind signals, ending in a shadowgraph. One frontispiece line vows to spend a fortune finding a man and hanging him, which promises railroad-country revenge without delivering the story.
the-young-engineers-in-nevada-or-seeking:
Tom Reade meets a dough-faced boy of fourteen in The Young Engineers in Nevada, by H. Irving Hancock. The boy, Alf, asks whether Tom has the makings. He means tobacco makings, a bid toward manhood. Tom glances up in mild astonishment inside the tent. The contents promise gold fever, claim jumping, and wolves on snow. Jim Ferrers becomes the boys' partner in mining.

Nevada gold replaces railroads as the young engineers' pursuit. A goddess of fortune smiles wistfully in one chapter title. Dolph Gage fires a shot in another. Hancock mixes mining know-how with fights and rescues. Series readers follow Reade and Hazelton across the whole American West.
wild-western-scenes-a-narrative-of-adven: The title pages here give a full promise of contents for J. B. Jones's Wild Western Scenes, but the narrative itself does not start. Lippincott printed a revised stereotype edition in Philadelphia in 1875; Jones entered the book for copyright in 1856. The title page pledges tales of Daniel Boone, the great pioneer. It also promises bear, deer, and buffalo hunts, fights, wolf hunts, fishing, and encounters with serpents. Sixteen engravings from original designs illustrate the book. A preface begins at the foot of the pages shown.
woodside-or-look-listen-and-learn: Caroline Hadley wrote this children's nature book, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1902. Pages present here hold illustrated title pages and the start of a verse motto about Nature as an old nurse. The motto invites a child to wander and read the book of the natural world. Listed pictures promise a visit to a watchdog and an arrival at grandpapa's house. No story chapters appear in these pages.
